enrichment.short_title: Somali asylum seeker's Article 8 judicial review fails where section 72 certification upheld despite identity dispute
key_facts: Somali national entered the UK in December 2001 after three and a half years in Italy, claiming asylum and later an Article 8 right to remain with her refugee mother in the UK.

The Secretary of State certified her human rights appeal as manifestly unfounded under section 72(2)(a) and maintained that decision after DNA evidence confirmed maternity; disputes remained over identity, age, and credibility.

She entered by deception using Italian documents in the name Sadia Mohamed Hassan while claiming to be Sadia Abdulkadir A born in 1984; the Home Office said return to Italy was proportionate and she should have applied for entry clearance honestly.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of the Secretary of State's certification under section 72(2)(a) of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 that the claimant's Article 8 allegation was manifestly unfounded.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the court held the Secretary of State was entitled to certify the human rights claim as manifestly unfounded even accepting the claimant's account of age and identity; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 72 certification requires that no adjudicator could find a breach of Article 8; where a claimant entered by deception to circumvent entry clearance, maintained firm immigration control is a proportionate interference with family life even if family links exist, and an adjudicator could not be bound to find a breach on the assumed facts.
legal_issues: Whether the Secretary of State could rationally certify the Article 8 claim as manifestly unfounded under section 72(2)(a)
Whether an adjudicator would be bound to disbelieve the claimant on age and identity
Whether return to Italy would breach Article 8 even if the claimant were a minor dependent of a refugee mother
Whether the safe third country family links policy was relevant to section 72 certification
Whether lack of identification documents in Italy prevented proportionate insistence on entry clearance

enrichment.short_title: Caravan site company qualifies for 100% business property relief where services predominate over land letting

statutes_considered.title: Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960

key_facts: Executors appealed against Laddie J's reversal of a Special Commissioner's decision denying business property relief on 85% shareholding in Dunton Park Caravan Sites Limited.

The company operated a residential mobile homes park, caravan storage, a country club, utility resale, and caravan sales; the dispute centred on whether the business consisted mainly of holding investments.
The Special Commissioner found residential park services predominated over the investment element of plot lettings; the High Court had treated ancillary services as part of the investment business.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from a High Court decision reversing the Special Commissioner's inheritance tax decision on business property relief.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Special Commissioner's decision restored and 100% business property relief held available on the share transfer.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 105(3) IHTA 1984 the question whether a caravan site business consists mainly of holding investments is primarily one of fact for the Special Commissioner; additional services such as utility supply and site management are not necessarily incidental to letting merely because required by licence or agreement, and lease terms are not definitive of character.
legal_issues: Whether Dunton Park Caravan Sites Limited carried on a business consisting wholly or mainly of making or holding investments
How to classify residential caravan park services versus plot-letting income
Whether activities required by site licence or occupier agreements are investment or trading activities
Whether the Special Commissioner's factual approach involved an error of law

enrichment.short_title: Foreign corporation need not prove actual financial loss to maintain English libel claim after Human Rights Act
key_facts: At a pre-trial review before trial of a libel claim by Jameel and a Saudi company against The Wall Street Journal Europe, the defendants sought to strike out the second claimant on a preliminary basis.
Mr Robertson QC argued that after the Human Rights Act 1998 a foreign corporation must prove measurable damage to trading reputation rather than rely on the presumption of damage.

The claimants contended Article 10 did not require that modification and that corporations, like individuals, could obtain vindication through modest or nominal damages where financial loss was not shown.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Pre-trial review in the Queen's Bench Division on a preliminary issue whether a foreign corporate libel claimant must prove special damage under Article 10.
enrichment.outcome: Preliminary submission rejected; second claimant permitted to remain in proceedings at least for the time being; standing and reputation issues left for later determination.
enrichment.ratio: Article 10 does not require foreign corporations with a recognised cause of action in defamation to prove actual financial loss before recovering damages for vindication; the long-standing presumption of damage remains compatible with Convention values and proportionate remedies.
legal_issues: Whether a foreign corporation must prove special or measurable damage to maintain a libel claim after the Human Rights Act 1998
Whether the presumption of damage in corporate defamation survives Article 10 scrutiny
Whether vindication through damages requires proof of pecuniary loss for corporate claimants
Whether foreign and domestic corporations should be treated differently for this purpose

enrichment.short_title: Sudanese asylum seeker's judicial review dismissed despite hardship findings and later family life in UK
key_facts: Sudanese claimant arrived in July 2001, was refused asylum, and failed before an adjudicator and the Immigration Appeal Tribunal; she later married a fellow Sudanese asylum seeker and had a child.
The adjudicator accepted a traumatic history in Sudan but found she left for economic reasons and would face hardship, not Convention persecution or Article 3 ill-treatment, on return to Khartoum.

Fresh representations and a section 96(2) certificate were challenged together with the IAT refusal of permission; the Secretary of State relied on country information denying systematic mistreatment of failed asylum seekers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review challenging the IAT's refusal of permission to appeal, fresh asylum/human rights decisions, and certification under section 96(2) of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; challenge to IAT/adjudicator decisions and October 2003 Home Office decisions rejected; section 96 certification upheld; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: New internal relocation and social-group arguments raised late were not arguable errors; hardship and displacement findings insufficient for Article 3, and Article 8 added nothing where treatment fell short of Article 3 severity; section 96(2) properly applied to repeated grounds and family-life matters that should have been raised earlier.

Whether internal relocation to Khartoum should have been assessed under the unduly harsh test
Whether the claimant qualified as a member of a particular social group
Whether section 96(2) certification was lawful for repeated and previously omitted grounds

enrichment.short_title: Inspector lawfully refused section 73 time extension despite section 106 land transfer to parish council
key_facts: Outline permission for seven bungalows expired for reserved matters approval; successor developer applied under section 73 to extend time after acquiring the site.
A section 106 agreement required transfer of adjoining land to the parish council for £1 and imposed drainage obligations if residential development caused flooding.

The Inspector refused the section 73 application because changed national and local policy under PPG3 made greenfield development objectionable; the High Court quashed that decision for failing to weigh the developer's continuing obligations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal by the First Secretary of State against a High Court section 288 quashing of an Inspector's refusal of a section 73 application to extend time for reserved matters approval.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Inspector's decision restored and statutory challenge dismissed with costs.
enrichment.ratio: Completion of a section 106 land transfer does not create a legitimate expectation of indefinite planning permission; a continuing drainage obligation under the agreement was not a material factor against refusal where development could not lawfully proceed, and an Inspector aware of the agreement is presumed to have taken relevant obligations into account.
legal_issues: Whether the Inspector erred by failing to consider the developer's continuing section 106 drainage obligation
Whether transfer of adjoining land created a legitimate expectation of extending outline permission
Whether planning history and the section 106 bargain required grant of the section 73 application
How current planning policy may be taken into account on a section 73 application

enrichment.short_title: Interim ASBO batch procedure upheld but Luke Kenny's order quashed for lack of individual evidence
key_facts: Leeds City Council and West Yorkshire Police obtained without-notice interim ASBOs against 66 individuals in Operation Cape targeting drug dealing and associated disorder in Little London, Leeds.
Claimants challenged the lawfulness of Rule 5 without-notice interim ASBO procedure and the evidential basis for orders against them individually.
Luke Kenny was 17 when the order was made; evidence against him was largely general association and incidents outside the exclusion zone, described as guilt by association.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated judicial review of interim anti-social behaviour orders made without notice under section 1D Crime and Disorder Act 1998, with permission and substantive hearing heard together.
enrichment.outcome: Rule 5 without-notice interim ASBO procedure held lawful and not a determination under Article 6; M's claim dismissed; Luke Kenny granted permission and his interim ASBO discharged as unsupported by evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Interim ASBOs made without notice are lawful interim measures that do not determine civil rights under Article 6 until the substantive hearing; the section 1D test is whether it is just to make an order pending the main application, but each defendant must have an individual evidential basis and the burden remains on the applicant on discharge applications.

Whether an interim ASBO without notice is a determination of civil rights
What test applies to granting interim ASBOs under section 1D
Whether batch without-notice orders against 66 defendants were justified
Whether there was sufficient evidence to make or maintain the orders against each claimant

enrichment.short_title: Council's under-occupation possession claim fails where tenant's right to buy was deliberately stalled
key_facts: Secure tenant of a three-bedroom Kensington maisonette succeeded her mother and served a section 122 right-to-buy notice; the borough admitted her right but deliberately refused to serve the section 125 purchase terms notice.
The borough then brought possession proceedings on Ground 16 under-occupation, offering alternative two-bedroom accommodation at substantially higher rent.
The tenant lived with her sister and nephew; the county court held it unreasonable to order possession because the council had prevented her exercising the statutory right to buy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea against dismissal of its secure tenancy possession claim based on under-occupation (Ground 16).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; possession order refused as unreasonable where the landlord deliberately failed to comply with section 125 and thwarted the tenant's right to buy.
enrichment.ratio: Where possession and an in-progress right to buy conflict, reasonableness under section 84(2)(c) may take account of the tenant's established right to buy; a local authority's deliberate failure to serve mandatory section 125 notices can make possession unreasonable even if possession would otherwise be arguable.
legal_issues: How courts should resolve conflicts between a landlord's possession claim and a tenant's partially exercised right to buy
Whether the borough's failure to serve a section 125 notice was relevant to reasonableness under Ground 16
What factors bear on reasonableness under section 84(2)(c) where right to buy is pending
Whether alternative accommodation offered was suitable under Part IV Schedule 2

enrichment.short_title: English declaratory claim over LPG joint venture memorandum stayed pending Texas forum ruling
key_facts: BP International and Energy Infrastructure Group entered a July 1998 English-law memorandum for an Indian LPG joint venture through Wimco Petrogas; negotiations for a shareholders' agreement failed and the memorandum expired in January 1999.

EIG sued BPI in Dallas for over US$100 million alleging fraud and breach of fiduciary duty; BPI then commenced English proceedings seeking negative declarations limiting contractual liability under clauses 5 and 13.
BPI had submitted to Texas jurisdiction under a procedural agreement while pursuing forum non conveniens; the English claim was largely contrived to support the Texas dismissal application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court application under CPR Part 11 to set aside service out of the jurisdiction and/or stay English declaratory proceedings pending resolution of parallel Texas litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Serious issue to be tried found and service not set aside for non-disclosure; English proceedings stayed until the Dallas court ruled on BPI's forum non conveniens motion.
enrichment.ratio: A non-exclusive English jurisdiction clause permits declaratory proceedings where a genuine contractual dispute exists, but where parallel Texas tort proceedings overlap and the claimant has submitted to Texas jurisdiction, the court may stay English proceedings as an exceptional case to avoid conflicting litigation.

enrichment.short_title: US boxing judgment enforceable in England except trebled RICO damages under Protection of Trading Interests Act

statutes_considered.title: Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act

key_facts: Lennox Lewis obtained a US$7,273,641 judgment in New York against his former managers Panos Eliades and Panix companies for fraud, breach of fiduciary duty, and RICO violations.
The jury awarded US$396,082 basic RICO damages later trebled in a consolidated nunc pro tunc judgment to US$8,065,805 including US$1,188,246 trebled RICO damages.
Defendants argued the entire judgment was unenforceable under section 5 PTIA because RICO provides automatic treble recovery.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against refusal to set aside summary judgment enforcing the New York judgment at common law under CPR Part 24.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed in part; composite judgment enforceable except the trebled RICO element, yielding net enforceable sum of US$5,877,559 after agreed set-off.
enrichment.ratio: Section 5(3) PTIA precludes enforcement only to the extent a foreign judgment is for an amount arrived at by multiplying assessed compensation; where a composite judgment includes both ordinary compensatory awards and a multiplied RICO element, the non-multiplied parts remain enforceable at common law.
legal_issues: Whether section 5 PTIA bars enforcement of an entire composite US judgment containing trebled RICO damages
How to construe 'a judgment for multiple damages' in section 5(3)
Whether the basic compensatory RICO award is separately enforceable
Whether the New York judgment was final and conclusive for enforcement purposes
